source: Ericsson, Krampe, Tesch-Romer (1993) The role of deliberate practice (as reported in the 2019 replication)
finding: Berlin violinists: more accumulated solitary practice to age 18 went with higher skill group. This is the founding claim of the deliberate-practice view.
numbers: Practice alone to age 18: best M=7410 h, good M=5301 h, less accomplished M=3420 h. Ericsson (2014) later gave the best group's 95% CI as 2894-11926 h.
limits: Numbers seen only as quoted in the replication paper, not the 1993 text. Retrospective estimates. Small groups. The best-vs-good test was reported as p<.05 only.
agent_relevance: Practice type (structured, goal-directed, with feedback) is the idea to borrow, not the hours count.

source: Macnamara & Maitra (2019) The role of deliberate practice in expert performance: revisiting Ericsson et al. 1993
finding: Double-blind replication with violin students did not replicate the core finding that accumulated practice matches each skill level.
numbers: Accumulated practice alone to age 18: group effect eta2=0.26 (p=0.001), but best (M=8224, CI 6400-10048) did NOT beat good (M=9844, CI 6937-12751), t(24)=-0.93, p=0.364, d=-0.38. Good beat less accomplished (M=4558), d=1.33, p=0.005. Weekly practice alone: F(2,36)=27.36, eta2=0.60. By age 20 best and good both above 10,000 h on average.
quote: We did not replicate the core finding that accumulated amounts of deliberate practice corresponded to each skill level.
limits: Roughly 39 violinists (df implies this). Retrospective self-report. Effect substantial but much smaller than original. Teacher-designed practice (closest to the theory's definition) did not explain more variance than practice alone.
agent_relevance: Volume of practice separates levels only up to a point; a loop that just adds attempts is not enough.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick, Oswald (2014) Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis
finding: Deliberate practice explained a moderate share of skill differences in games, much less elsewhere.
numbers: Variance explained: games 26%, music 21%, sports 18%, education 4%, professions under 1%.
quote: deliberate practice is important, but not as important as has been argued
limits: Abstract text only (read via Europe PMC), not the full paper. Self-reported practice. Games includes chess. Ericsson and colleagues disputed the definition of deliberate practice used.
agent_relevance: Even in games about three-quarters of skill variance is not tied to accumulated practice time; practice quality and other factors matter.

source: Macnamara, Moreau, Hambrick (2016) The relationship between deliberate practice and performance in sports: a meta-analysis
finding: Practice explains less as skill level rises: nearly nothing among elites.
numbers: Overall 18% of variance in sports performance; 1% among elite performers. High-skill athletes did not start earlier than lower-skill athletes.
limits: Abstract only. Sports, not chess.
agent_relevance: Marginal gains from more practice shrink near the top; fits diminishing returns from extra self-improvement rounds.

source: Dutch longitudinal study (2008) Deliberate practice predicts performance over time in adolescent chess players and drop-outs
finding: Linear mixed models on young Dutch elite chess players: serious solitary study and serious play strongly predicted rating over careers, to the same degree in persisters and drop-outs.
numbers: Abstract gives no effect sizes. Gender effect was much smaller than the practice effect.
limits: Abstract only; authors not recorded this session. Observational, so talent and practice may be confounded.
agent_relevance: Supports the monotonic-benefit assumption in chess specifically.

source: Chess.com cohort (2026) Not All Practice Is Created Equal: Longitudinal evidence from over 40,000 chess players
finding: Time-stamped logs: practice-aligned activities gave far more rating gain per unit time than playing games, though most time went into games.
numbers: N=44,213 Chess.com players. Over 90% of time spent on games. Deliberate-practice-aligned activities: 3.61x learning-efficiency advantage over gameplay (ps<.001); not all such activities were equally effective.
limits: Abstract only. Observational; self-selection into practice types. Journal and authors not recorded.
agent_relevance: Strongest recent chess evidence that practice TYPE beats volume. Argues for targeted drills with feedback in an agent loop, not more free play.

source: Jones (2021) Scaling Scaling Laws with Board Games (AlphaZero on Hex)
finding: Self-play skill follows smooth compute laws; train-time and test-time compute trade off.
numbers: In the linear regime 500 Elo per 10x compute (about 2x the compute of an opponent wins 2/3 of games). Compute for perfect play grows 7x per board-size step; takeoff compute 4x.
limits: Hex, not chess. Small boards, in-house AlphaZero implementation.
agent_relevance: Machine practice amount has a clean law; human practice hours do not. Useful contrast.

source: Silver et al. (2017) Mastering chess and shogi by self-play with a general RL algorithm (AlphaZero)
finding: Self-play with no human data reached superhuman chess in hours.
numbers: Beat Stockfish after about 4 hours (300k steps); Go: beat AlphaGo Lee after 8 hours; shogi: beat Elmo in under 2 hours. 100-game match vs Stockfish: AlphaZero lost zero games.
limits: Large TPU compute. Self-play is practice at the edge of own ability but needs a verifiable win signal.
agent_relevance: Self-play against a copy of oneself is the machine form of deliberate practice; needs a ground-truth outcome check.

source: McIlroy-Young, Sen, Kleinberg, Anderson (2020) Aligning superhuman AI with human behavior: chess as a model system (Maia)
finding: Engines tuned for strength do not predict human moves well; models trained on human games at one rating level do.
numbers: Leela best move-matching 46%; Maia (trained per rating band 1100-1900; 12M games for 1100, 120k for 1900) reaches over 52% at best; Maia 1900 predicting 1100 players about 46%. Stockfish matching is nearly flat across skill (about 40%).
limits: Predicts moves; does not model learning. Lichess blitz/rapid data.
agent_relevance: A student model for each skill level can pick practice at the right difficulty and predict likely mistakes.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess
finding: A 270M transformer trained by supervised distillation of Stockfish values plays at grandmaster level without search.
numbers: 10M games, about 15B data points. Tournament Elo 9M 2025, 136M 2259, 270M 2299; Lichess blitz vs humans 2895; puzzle accuracy 88.9/94.5/95.4%. AlphaZero policy-only 1777, 56.1% puzzles.
limits: Elo vs bots lower than vs humans. Stockfish oracle labels, so not self-practice. Authors say perfect distillation is futile at this scale.
agent_relevance: Strength came from huge numbers of labelled positions (feedback at every position), a data-side analogue of immediate feedback.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) same paper, general-LLM row (GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct)
finding: A general text-trained language model, given the whole game in PGN, played far below the specialised model.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct: Lichess Elo about 1755 vs bots; 66.5% puzzle accuracy; versus 2299 and 95.4% for the 270M specialised model.
limits: Authors skipped GPT-4 because earlier work found it made illegal moves. One model, no prompt variants tested.
agent_relevance: Without feedback-heavy training, general models lag in chess; a scaffold must supply state checking and move legality.

source: Toshniwal, Wiseman, Livescu, Gimpel (2022) Chess as a testbed for language model state tracking
finding: Transformers trained on move text alone track pieces and predict legal moves with enough data; small data needs board-state hints; full attention is needed.
numbers: Piece-location tracking about 99% with the large training set; accuracy dropped for approximate-attention transformers and LSTMs.
limits: Small LMs trained from scratch, not prompted frontier models. Exact legal-move percentages not extracted.
agent_relevance: Exposing board state during training helps; for an agent, explicit state tracking beats remembering move lists.

source: ChessGPT paper (2023) bridging policy learning and language modeling
finding: Dataset mixing game replays and chess-language text trained ChessGPT and ChessCLIP; includes an evaluation framework for state tracking, value judging and policy.
numbers: Exact scores not extracted this session.
limits: Authors not recorded. Tables not read in detail.
agent_relevance: Language commentary plus game records together act like coach feedback.

source: Zelikman, Wu, Mu, Goodman (2022) STaR: bootstrapping reasoning with reasoning
finding: Loop: attempt, keep rationales that reach the right answer, retrain; for failures, rerun with the answer as a hint (rationalization).
numbers: Arithmetic after 16 iterations 89.5% vs 76.3% for answer-only fine-tune. GSM8K: few-shot CoT 36.6, direct fine-tune 60.0, STaR 68.8, STaR+rationalization 72.5. CommonsenseQA +35.9 over few-shot, +12.5 over direct fine-tune; comparable to a 30x larger fine-tuned model.
limits: GPT-J 6B. Needs verifiable answers.
agent_relevance: Retry-with-hint on failures, then keep what worked, is usable as a pattern.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Self-play fine-tuning converts weak language models to strong language models (SPIN)
finding: A model improves by telling its own earlier outputs from human data, round after round, with no new human labels.
numbers: Open LLM Leaderboard average 58.14 to 63.16 using only a 50k data subset.
limits: Gains level off over iterations. Needs a reference standard to play against. Authors list not recorded.
agent_relevance: Self-play practice is possible for text agents when a reference standard exists.

source: An et al. (2023) Learning from mistakes makes LLM better reasoner (LeMa)
finding: Fine-tuning on mistake-and-correction pairs written by GPT-4 beats fine-tuning on correct chains alone.
numbers: LLaMA-2-70B: GSM8K 83.5% vs 81.4% CoT-only; MATH 25.0% vs 23.6%; with correction-centric evolution MATH 29.3%.
limits: Plain gains are only 1.4-2.1 points; corrections come from a stronger model. Authors list approximate.
agent_relevance: Error-focused practice helps modestly and needs a stronger corrector.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning
finding: Agent writes a verbal reflection after a failed attempt and keeps it in memory for the next try.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%; ALFWorld +22% absolute in 12 steps; HotPotQA +20%.
limits: No weight updates. Needs a usable failure signal such as tests or environment reward.
agent_relevance: Retry with reflection is the in-loop version of practice with feedback.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with large language models
finding: Automatic curriculum proposes the next task by current skill, plus a growing skill library and self-verification.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 iterations (3.3x baselines); wooden/stone/iron tools 15.3x/8.5x/6.4x faster; only agent reaching diamond. Random curriculum cut discovered items by 93%.
limits: Minecraft with GPT-4. Part of the gain is the skill library.
agent_relevance: Choosing tasks at the edge of ability is what deliberate practice calls for; random order destroyed 93% of progress.

source: Jiang, Grefenstette, Rocktaschel (2021) Prioritized level replay
finding: Replaying levels with highest estimated learning potential improves sample efficiency and generalization.
numbers: Procgen: UCB-DrAC+PLR gave 76% improvement in mean test return over PPO with uniform sampling and 28% over previous best; PLR with rank prioritization significant gains on 10 of 16 games.
limits: Reinforcement learning, not language models. Author names from memory of the paper header, not checked.
agent_relevance: Machine counterpart of choosing practice just beyond current skill.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Skill-it: a data-driven skills framework for understanding and training language models
finding: Skills have a learning order; sampling training data by prerequisite skills teaches advanced skills with less data.
numbers: LEGO synthetic: +36.5 points vs random sampling. Natural Instructions: 13.6% lower validation loss on target skill. 3B model with 1B tokens beat uniform sampling at 3B tokens on LM Evaluation Harness.
limits: Skills are defined by the data. Authors not recorded.
agent_relevance: Order and targeting of practice beat volume, matching the practice-type claim.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: Best use of extra thinking time depends on prompt difficulty; allocate it adaptively.
numbers: Compute-optimal strategy over 4x more efficient than best-of-N; in FLOPs-matched tests a smaller model with test-time compute beat a 14x larger model on problems where it has non-trivial success.
limits: Math with verifier models. Not practice as such.
agent_relevance: Spend effort where success is partial, the same logic as practicing at the edge of ability.

source: Schut, Tomasev, McGrath, Hassabis, Paquet, Kim (2023) Bridging the human-AI knowledge gap: concept discovery and transfer in AlphaZero
finding: Concepts mined from AlphaZero were taught to top grandmasters, who then solved concept puzzles better.
numbers: 4 grandmasters (one rated 2600-2700, three 2700-2800). Percent correct, phase 1 to phase 3 (parsed from a garbled table, row order uncertain): gains of +42, +25, +16 and +6 points, e.g. 0 to 42 and 33 to 58. Gain did not track rating.
limits: Four participants; no control group; puzzles chosen by the system. Not an LLM.
agent_relevance: Machine-generated drills can move expert humans; a machine can be the coach.

source: Hicke et al. (2026) MedSimAI: simulation and formative feedback generation to enhance deliberate practice in medical education
finding: LLM patient simulator with structured rubric feedback deployed across three medical schools.
numbers: 410 students, 1,024 encounters, 30 cases. 59.5% did multiple encounters; 12 students (2.9%) did 8+ cases. At one site OSCE history-taking rose 82.8 to 88.8 (p<0.001, d=0.75); a second site's pilot showed no significant change. Automated scoring 87% accuracy on proficiency thresholds.
limits: Cohort comparison, not randomized; self-selected users; low usage; one site null.
agent_relevance: LLM-run practice with feedback can help humans, but results are fragile and site-dependent.

source: Song et al. (2026) CPX-MATE: AI-based OSCE platform during national licensure preparation
finding: Voice-based AI evaluator and virtual patient used voluntarily before the Korean national OSCE; repeat practice gave small score gains.
numbers: 43 of 72 eligible students used it; adoption 97.7%; 3,042 sessions over 745.1 h; median 16.0 h and 66.5 sessions per user. 776 repeat pairs: second score +1.67 points (95% CI 0.99-2.23, p<0.001), mostly history taking.
limits: No control group; self-selected; one institution; scored by the same AI. Authors list many limitations.
agent_relevance: Repeat practice with automated feedback gave only a small gain.

source: Ma, Shen, Koedinger, Wu (2023) HypoCompass: LLMs as teachable agents for debugging
finding: Novices practice hypothesizing about bugs by helping an LLM teachable agent; the LLM makes the bugs and fixes.
numbers: 19 participants; pre-to-post test +11.7% (p=0.033); completion time -13.6%; LLM-made training material four times more efficient than human-made.
limits: Tiny sample, no control arm, 20-minute tests.
agent_relevance: LLMs can supply practice items at graded difficulty.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Bridging VLMs and embodied intelligence with Deliberate Practice Policy Optimization (DPPO)
finding: Training loop alternates RL (low success rate exposes weaknesses) and SFT (fixes them), named after deliberate practice.
numbers: Pelican-VL 1.0 72B: +20.3% over base; +10.6% over open models at 100B scale; DPPO +15.8% over RL alone with less forgetting; average +15.4% across nine reasoning dimensions.
limits: Authors' own benchmarks; link to Ericsson is by analogy. Embodied vision-language, not chess.
agent_relevance: Most explicit LLM use of the deliberate-practice idea: find weak spots by failure rate, then train on them.
